Textless variant cover of _Green Arrow_ (vol. 6) No. 1 (August 2016). Art by [Neal Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neal_Adams "Neal Adams").

In 2016, DC relaunched its entire line of titles once again with the [DC Rebirth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DC_Rebirth "DC Rebirth") event, this time intending to restore elements from the DC Universe prior to _Flashpoint_, while also maintaining the continuity of the New 52.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-30) Ben Percy remained the principal writer for the series, with a rotating art team consisting of Otto Schmidt, [Juan Ferreyra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_Ferreyra?action=edit&redlink=1 "Juan Ferreyra (page does not exist)") and [Stephen Byrne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Byrne_(comics) "Stephen Byrne (comics)"). During this run, Green Arrow is seemingly betrayed by Emiko as Percy reintroduces [Shado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shado_(comics) "Shado (comics)"), echoing elements from the Grell run, as well as [John Diggle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Diggle_(Arrowverse) "John Diggle (Arrowverse)"). In addition to restoring Green Arrow's trademark Van Dyke beard, the series revisited a romance between Green Arrow and Black Canary for the first time since 2011. Percy also reestablished Green Arrow as a politically conscious figure, with the writer describing him as a "[social justice warrior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_justice_warrior "Social justice warrior")".[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-31) After it was revealed that Emiko was still on Oliver's side, she eventually adopted the codename of _Red Arrow_.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-32)

This volume finished in March 2019, with issue No. 50 serving as an extra sized final issue.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-33)

### Dawn of DC

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Green_Arrow&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Dawn of DC")]

In November 2022, it was announced that [Joshua Williamson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Williamson "Joshua Williamson") would write a new Green Arrow series following Oliver's disappearance at the end of [_Dark Crisis on Infinite Earths_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_Crisis "Dark Crisis"), with Sean Izaakse illustrating and launching in April 2023.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-34) On April 25, the day of the first issue's release, it was announced that the initial six-issue miniseries would become a twelve-issue maxiseries.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-35)

Oliver eventually reunites with [Connor Hawke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connor_Hawke "Connor Hawke"), [Roy Harper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Harper_(character) "Roy Harper (character)"), [Black Canary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Canary "Black Canary"), Red Canary, and Liam Harper after defeating Merlyn. Oliver has seemingly worked with [Amanda Waller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amanda_Waller "Amanda Waller") and starts arresting his family.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-36) During his work with Waller, he digs up a box that seemingly makes him regain his memory. It is revealed that [Martian Manhunter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martian_Manhunter "Martian Manhunter") realized Amanda Waller's plans to make the world hate [metahumans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metahuman "Metahuman"), so he agreed to create a telepathic implant which will make Ollie fully believe in Waller's goals. Oliver helps disable the Amazon bots and the heroes regain their powers. In the aftermath, Oliver explains he had to do it because the Justice League disbanded so quickly when the Titans were not ready for future loose ends. He then further states that if they all had been more communicative as they did in the past, the events of Absolute Power would never had happened. [Batman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batman "Batman"), [Superman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superman "Superman"), and [Wonder Woman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wonder_Woman "Wonder Woman") begrudgingly agree with Oliver's reasonings and tell Oliver that they are bringing back the Justice League.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-37)

As with other DC superheroes, Green Arrow has an extensive supporting cast of characters, sometimes called **Team Arrow**, along with a unique [rogues gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rogues_gallery "Rogues gallery") of villains. His supporting cast has changed wildly over the course of the series, but has tended to include his sidekick [Speedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speedy_(comics) "Speedy (comics)") ([Roy Harper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Harper_(character) "Roy Harper (character)") and [Mia Dearden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mia_Dearden "Mia Dearden")) and his fellow superhero and main romantic interest, [Black Canary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Canary "Black Canary"). His son [Connor Hawke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connor_Hawke "Connor Hawke") has also been a part of the Arrow vigilante family, along with Black Canary's adopted daughter [Sin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sin_(DC_Comics) "Sin (DC Comics)"). For a brief time, Green Arrow was also "assisted" by the aspiring superhero [Miss Arrowette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrowette "Arrowette"), with whom he had a brief affair. The New 52 reboot of Green Arrow has also introduced a number of new supporting characters for Oliver, including ex-Queen Industries technology experts Naomi Singh and Henry Fyff, and his archer half-sister [Emiko Queen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emiko_Queen "Emiko Queen") who later takes up the code-name _Red Arrow_.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-38) The characters of [Felicity Smoak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felicity_Smoak "Felicity Smoak") and [John Diggle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Diggle_(Arrowverse) "John Diggle (Arrowverse)") from the _Arrow_ TV series were also adapted into the comic books in 2015 (though Felicity was later removed from the continuity). The archer [Shado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shado_(comics) "Shado (comics)"), though not part of Oliver's unit of heroes, has also been a recurring character in Oliver's life. Additionally, Green Arrow has been regularly paired with his fellow superhero [Green Lantern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Lantern "Green Lantern") ([Hal Jordan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hal_Jordan "Hal Jordan")) in comics, as the two co-starred in the series _Green Lantern/Green Arrow_ together for many years. The _[Arrow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrow\_(TV\_series) "Arrow (TV series)")_ version of Team Arrow include [Roy Harper/Arsenal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Harper_(Arrowverse) "Roy Harper (Arrowverse)"), [Sara Lance/White Canary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sara_Lance "Sara Lance"), [Thea Queen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thea_Queen "Thea Queen")/Speedy, [Laurel Lance/Black Canary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Lance_(Arrowverse) "Laurel Lance (Arrowverse)"), [Curtis Holt/Mister Terrific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curtis_Holt_(Arrowverse) "Curtis Holt (Arrowverse)"), [Rene Ramirez/Wild Dog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rene_Ramirez "Rene Ramirez"), [Rory Regan/Ragman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rory_Regan_(Arrowverse) "Rory Regan (Arrowverse)"), [Evelyn Sharp/Artemis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evelyn_Sharp_(Arrowverse) "Evelyn Sharp (Arrowverse)") and [Dinah Drake/Black Canary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinah_Drake_(Arrowverse) "Dinah Drake (Arrowverse)").

As a [Justice League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justice_League "Justice League") member, Green Arrow will also appear in crossovers with stories featuring other DC flagship characters from time to time. Of his Justice League colleagues, classic stories depict Ollie as having an ongoing feud with [Hawkman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawkman "Hawkman") owing to their differing outlooks on life, and more recently, he has been depicted as a good friend of his [Justice League United](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justice_League_United "Justice League United") colleague [Animal Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_Man "Animal Man"). Green Arrow has also been a member of the [Outsiders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outsiders_(comics) "Outsiders (comics)"), both in its incarnation as a covert superhero team led by [Batman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batman "Batman") and in its New 52 form as a [secret society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secret_society "Secret society") based around various weapon clans, including an Arrow Clan which Oliver is the rightful head of. In the [Golden Age of Comic Books](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Age_of_Comic_Books "Golden Age of Comic Books"), Green Arrow and Speedy were also affiliated with the superhero group the [Seven Soldiers of Victory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_Soldiers_of_Victory "Seven Soldiers of Victory").

### Enemies

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Green_Arrow&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Enemies")]

Recurring Green Arrow villains of course include his archenemies [Merlyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merlyn_(DC_Comics) "Merlyn (DC Comics)"), a master archer, and [Count Vertigo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_Vertigo "Count Vertigo"),[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-39) a foreign dignitary with the power to disrupt his enemy's balance and perception. Other recurring villains have included [China White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_White_(character) "China White (character)"), [Clock King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clock_King "Clock King"), [Cupid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cupid_(DC_Comics) "Cupid (DC Comics)"), [Brick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brick_(character) "Brick (character)"), and [Constantine Drakon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantine_Drakon "Constantine Drakon"). Since the 2000s, the longstanding DC supervillain [Deathstroke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deathstroke "Deathstroke") has often been depicted as having a particular grudge against Green Arrow.

### Earth-Two

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Green_Arrow&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Earth-Two")]

See also: [Crisis on Infinite Earths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crisis_on_Infinite_Earths "Crisis on Infinite Earths") and [Multiverse (DC Comics)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiverse_(DC_Comics) "Multiverse (DC Comics)")

For many years, DC Comics wrote stories in what it called a [multiverse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiverse "Multiverse"), or a series of infinite parallel Earths. This allowed DC writers to freely [retcon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retcon "Retcon") and retell stories, as well as explain continuity mistakes. The Green Arrow of the 1940s, like all [Golden Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Age_of_Comic_Books "Golden Age of Comic Books") characters at that time, resided on [Earth-Two](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth-Two "Earth-Two") and was a member of the [Seven Soldiers of Victory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_Soldiers_of_Victory "Seven Soldiers of Victory") and [All-Star Squadron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All-Star_Squadron "All-Star Squadron") along with his sidekick [Speedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Harper_(character) "Roy Harper (character)"). Despite having a different origin than the modern Green Arrow, the Golden Age character's development largely parallels the modern one's. In _[Crisis on Infinite Earths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crisis\_on\_Infinite\_Earths "Crisis on Infinite Earths")_, the multiverse is destroyed and Green Arrow is retroactively erased.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-42)

### Modern DC alternate universes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Green_Arrow&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Modern DC alternate universes")]

DC's weekly series _[52](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/52\_(comics) "52 (comics)")_ established a new 52-Earth [Multiverse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiverse_(DC_Comics) "Multiverse (DC Comics)"). The ongoing series _[Countdown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Countdown\_(DC\_Comics) "Countdown (DC Comics)")_ showcased several of these. On Earth-3, an evil equivalent of Oliver Queen is a member of the supervillain co-op called the [Crime Society of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crime_Syndicate "Crime Syndicate"). Another evil equivalent exists in the [Antimatter Universe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antimatter_universe_of_Qward "Antimatter universe of Qward") called **Deadeye**. On Earth-15, Roy Harper has replaced Oliver as Green Arrow.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-43) In the gender-reversed world of Earth-11, Oliver is now Olivia Queen, and that world's version of the Black Canary closely resembles him in appearance.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-44) The _Kingdom Come_ (Earth-22) and _Dark Knight Returns_ (Earth-31) stories and their variations of Oliver were later amalgamated into the 52-Earth Multiverse.

In the alternate timeline of the _[Flashpoint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flashpoint\_(comics) "Flashpoint (comics)")_ event, Oliver Queen is the head of Green Arrow Industries, a major military contracting company, as well as leads an ex-military band of Green Arrows. Even though Oliver is an inventive genius, he steals advanced gadgets from super-villains for military use. Oliver discovers his Green Arrows were killed by a female raider at his base at [Starfish Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Starfish_Island_(DC_Comics) "Starfish Island (DC Comics)") and killing his best friend/head of security Roy Harper. Taking his weapons and gadgets to hunt down the woman in battle, Oliver shockingly learns that she is a daughter of his and [Vixen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vixen_(character) "Vixen (character)"), Oliver's former lover, as well as the reason she attacked him was because Green Arrow Industries built factories which specializing in testing super-villain weapons in American towns that inadvertently became targets for the super-villains looking to gain their weapons back. Shocked by her revelation, Oliver had only been stalling before his daughter is killed by his reserve teams he earlier called.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-45)

### Earth-31/_The Dark Knight Returns_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Green_Arrow&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Earth-31/The Dark Knight Returns")]

The character appears in [Frank Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Miller "Frank Miller")'s _[Batman: The Dark Knight Returns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batman:\_The\_Dark\_Knight\_Returns "Batman: The Dark Knight Returns")_ and the sequel _[Batman: The Dark Knight Strikes Again](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batman:\_The\_Dark\_Knight\_Strikes\_Again "Batman: The Dark Knight Strikes Again")_ listed as [Earth-31](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth-31 "Earth-31"). Despite missing an arm (implied to be because of [Superman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superman "Superman")),[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-46) Oliver still proves to be an effective archer, grasping the nocks of his arrows in his teeth. After Batman fakes his death for him to go underground, Oliver, sporting a mechanical arm, joins Batman in his war against [Alexander Luthor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lex_Luthor "Lex Luthor")'s government. In _The Dark Knight Returns_, Oliver is portrayed as an anarchist, while in _The Dark Knight Strikes Again_, he is explicitly described as a "billionaire turned [Communist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communist "Communist")."[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-47)

### Other DC Elseworlds stories

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Green_Arrow&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Other DC Elseworlds stories")]

In _[JLA: The Nail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JLA:\_The\_Nail "JLA: The Nail")_ and [its sequel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JLA:_Another_Nail "JLA: Another Nail"), Oliver is a featured as a disabled ex-hero, having lost an arm, an eye, and the use of his legs in a fight with [Amazo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazo "Amazo"), which also resulted in the death of [Hawkman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawkman "Hawkman"). Bitter and furious, he now spreads fear on [Perry White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perry_White "Perry White")'s talk show about the JLA being aliens and claims that they are planning to conquer the world; his former teammates speculate that this is his method of coping.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-48) In the sequel, Oliver's brain is transplanted into Amazo's body–the Flash having removed Amazo's computerized brain in an earlier fight–restoring his sanity, allowing him to defeat the creature threatening the universe at the cost of his own life, after mending fences with his former teammates.

In _[Batman: Holy Terror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batman:\_Holy\_Terror "Batman: Holy Terror")_, Oliver Queen is mentioned as having been executed, found guilty of supporting underground Jewish "pornographers".[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-49) He has a cameo as Bruce Wayne's society friend in Dean Motter's _[Batman: Nine Lives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batman:\_Nine\_Lives "Batman: Nine Lives")_.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-50) Oliver Queen also appears in [Mike Mignola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Mignola "Mike Mignola")'s _[Batman: The Doom That Came to Gotham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batman:\_The\_Doom\_That\_Came\_to\_Gotham "Batman: The Doom That Came to Gotham")_, where he is portrayed as a guilt-ridden latter-day [Templar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knights_Templar "Knights Templar") equipped with magic arrows dipped in the blood of [Saint Sebastian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Sebastian "Saint Sebastian"). He is killed in issue No. 2 by [Poison Ivy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poison_Ivy_(character) "Poison Ivy (character)").[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-51) Oliver appears in _[Superman: Red Son](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superman:\_Red\_Son "Superman: Red Son")_, where Oliver Queen is a reporter for the _[Daily Planet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daily\_Planet "Daily Planet")_ working underneath [Perry White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perry_White "Perry White") and eventually [Lois Lane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lois_Lane "Lois Lane").[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-52)

An older, balding Green Arrow appears in [Mark Waid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Waid "Mark Waid") and [Alex Ross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Ross "Alex Ross")' futuristic _[Kingdom Come](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom\_Come\_(comics) "Kingdom Come (comics)")_, in which Oliver has joined forces with Batman to oppose Superman's army/Justice League. He married his longtime love [Dinah Lance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinah_Lance "Dinah Lance") and they have a daughter, **Olivia Queen** aka **Black Canary**.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-53)

Green Arrow appears in _League of Justice_, a _[The Lord of the Rings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Lord\_of\_the\_Rings "The Lord of the Rings")_–inspired fantasy where the character is renamed "**Longbow Greenarrow**": a mysterious wizard resembling [Gandalf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gandalf "Gandalf"). _JLA: Age of Wonder_ shows Green Arrow as a defender of the poor and an enemy of oppression.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-54)

### _Injustice_ series

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Green_Arrow&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Injustice series")]

In the _[Injustice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Injustice:\_Gods\_Among\_Us\_(comics) "Injustice: Gods Among Us (comics)")_ universe, where the [Joker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joker_(character) "Joker (character)") kills Lois Lane and her unborn child, Green Arrow joins Batman's Insurgency against Superman's Regime, recognizing Superman's harsher approach to ending crime following his loss. In _[Injustice: Gods Among Us](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Injustice:\_Gods\_Among\_Us\_(comics) "Injustice: Gods Among Us (comics)")_, Green Arrow is married to [Black Canary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Canary "Black Canary") and also unintentionally becomes close to [Harley Quinn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harley_Quinn "Harley Quinn"), who he saves from a near-death encounter with Superman. Near the end of Year One (the comic's first volume) he is mortally wounded by Superman in his Fortress of Solitude after the former mistakenly believes that the Insurgency has come to harm [Jonathan and Martha Kent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_and_Martha_Kent "Jonathan and Martha Kent"). Before dying, Green Arrow delivers the super pills to the Insurgency. Year Two reveals Black Canary to be pregnant with Green Arrow's child, leaving her determined to take down Superman for his murder.

*   When Superman nearly kills Black Canary trying to avenge Green Arrow, Doctor Fate heals and takes Dinah to an alternate universe where a different version of Oliver Queen remains alive but his own Black Canary, along with most of his allies, are deceased. Doctor Fate leaves the two to raise the baby—named [Conner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connor_Hawke "Connor Hawke")—together, giving each other a chance at happiness. Five years later, in the prequel comic of the game's sequel _[Injustice 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Injustice\_2\_(comics) "Injustice 2 (comics)")_, the alternate Oliver and Dinah receive news from Doctor Fate of Superman's defeat at the hands of his Prime-Earth counterpart. While Dinah is brought home by Doctor Fate to help Batman restore Earth, the alternate Oliver joins in to honor his late-counterpart. The alternate Oliver discovers that, unlike himself, his deceased counterpart maintained his wealth and resources, and while the public is unaware that its Oliver Queen is dead, alternate Green Arrow is able to access them for the heroes' needs. He learns his counterpart's marriage to Dinah, prompting her to ask the alternate Green Arrow his hand-in-marriage, which he accepts. He and Batman also do not get along, waiting for an opportunity to duel after Oliver reveals that, based on what he learned from Dinah, he has more training than his counterpart.

### Superman: American Alien

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Green_Arrow&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: Superman: American Alien")]

In the 2016 comic book _[Superman: American Alien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superman:\_American\_Alien "Superman: American Alien")_ by [Max Landis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Landis "Max Landis"), which features an alternate retelling of Clark's journey to becoming Superman, Oliver Queen encounters [Clark Kent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superman "Superman") two times in his life. First is when Clark was nineteen and Oliver mistakes him for [Bruce Wayne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batman "Batman"), whom he had thrown a birthday party for despite being aware that Wayne would never show up. Clark, after some hesitation, decides to enjoy himself and befriends Oliver, though he briefly becomes annoyed and shocked at how much money Oliver and his friends waste. Years later, after getting off Starfish Island, Oliver has matured more and encounters Clark again, who has begun his new career at the Daily Planet. At first believing him to be Bruce, Clark quickly comes clean. Oliver forgives him before introducing him to [Lex Luthor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lex_Luthor "Lex Luthor"), partly to annoy the latter.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-55)

### Earth 2

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Green_Arrow&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: Earth 2")]

In the pages of _[Earth 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth-Two "Earth-Two"): World's End_, Oliver Queen is an ally of Batman and operates as Red Arrow. When Batman was killed during the [Apokoliptian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apokolips "Apokolips") invasion, Red Arrow continued to guard the Codex, which contained the DNA of every organism on Earth, in an underwater fortress built by Bruce Wayne. When [Batman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Wayne "Thomas Wayne") and [Huntress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huntress_(Helena_Wayne) "Huntress (Helena Wayne)") arrive at the underwater fortress, they meet Red Arrow, who assists in fighting the second Apokoliptian invasion. Red Arrow and the Codex are evacuated from Earth before it is destroyed.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-56)

### Absolute Universe

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Green_Arrow&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: Absolute Universe")]

Two versions of Green Arrow appear in the [Absolute Universe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolute_Universe "Absolute Universe"), otherwise known as **Alpha World**, a universe corrupted by Darkseid's energy. In this world, Oliver Queen is a self-made billionaire who developed a trading app with his friend Jubal Slade, who he later cut ties with once he discovers Jubal's sexual misconduct. Years later, Oliver discovers Jubal's human trafficking operation on a remote island and plans to become a vigilante archer to take him down. However, his plans are discovered by the Justice League, who send [Carter Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carter_Hall_(comics) "Carter Hall (comics)") to assassinate him, ending his superhero career before it's begun.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-57)

Months later, a mysterious masked figure, dubbed **the Longbow Hunter**, appears wielding Oliver's gear and begins violently murdering corrupt billionaires connected to Oliver Queen, starting with Jubal Slade. Executive protection specialist and Oliver's ex-girlfriend, [Dinah Lance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinah_Lance "Dinah Lance"), is forcibly hired to investigate the Hunter and uncover his identity.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-58)

**Green Arrow** is a [superhero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superhero "Superhero") who appears in [American comic books](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_comic_books "American comic books") published by [DC Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DC_Comics "DC Comics"). Created by [Mort Weisinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mort_Weisinger "Mort Weisinger") and designed by [George Papp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Papp "George Papp"), he first appeared in _[More Fun Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/More\_Fun\_Comics "More Fun Comics")_ No. 73 on September 19, 1941 ([cover dated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cover_date "Cover date") November 1941), the same issue that debuted Aquaman. His [real name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secret_identity "Secret identity") is **Oliver Jonas "Ollie" Queen**, a wealthy businessman, owner of Queen Industries, and a well-known celebrity in [Star City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_City_(comics) "Star City (comics)"). He uses this position to hide the fact that he is Green Arrow.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-dc-ency-1) Partly inspired by [Robin Hood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Hood "Robin Hood"), Green Arrow is an [archer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery "Archery") who uses his skills to fight crime in his home cities of Star City and [Seattle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle "Seattle"), as well as alongside his fellow [superheroes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superhero "Superhero") as a member of the [Justice League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justice_League "Justice League"). The world's greatest archer, as well as a competent [swordsman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swordsmanship "Swordsmanship") and [martial artist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martial_arts "Martial arts"), Green Arrow deploys a range of trick arrows (in contemporary times, they are referred as "specialty arrows"[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-2)) with various special functions, such as [glue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glue "Glue"), explosive-tipped, grappling hook, [flash grenade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stun_grenade "Stun grenade"), [tear gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tear_gas "Tear gas"), and even [kryptonite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kryptonite "Kryptonite") arrows for use in a range of special situations.

Green Arrow enjoyed moderate success in his early years, becoming the cover feature of _More Fun_, as well as having occasional appearances in other comics. Throughout his first twenty-five years, however, the character never enjoyed greater popularity. In the late 1960s, writer [Denny O'Neil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denny_O'Neil "Denny O'Neil"), inspired by the character's dramatic visual redesign by [Neal Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neal_Adams "Neal Adams"), chose to have him lose his fortune, giving him the then-unique role of a streetwise crusader for the working class and the disadvantaged. In 1970, he was paired with a more law and order–oriented hero, [Green Lantern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hal_Jordan "Hal Jordan"), in a ground-breaking, socially conscious comic book series.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-3) Since then, he has been popular among comic book fans and most writers have taken an urban, gritty approach to the character. Oliver Queen was [killed off](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kill_off "Kill off") in the 1990s and replaced by a new character, Oliver's son [Connor Hawke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow_(Connor_Hawke) "Green Arrow (Connor Hawke)"). Connor, however, proved a less popular character, and the original Oliver Queen character was resurrected in the 2001 ["Quiver" storyline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quiver_(comics) "Quiver (comics)"), by writer [Kevin Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Smith "Kevin Smith"). In the 2000s, the character has been featured in bigger storylines focusing on Green Arrow and [Black Canary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Canary "Black Canary"), such as the DC event _The Green Arrow/Black Canary Wedding_ and the high-profile _[Justice League: Cry for Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justice\_League:\_Cry\_for\_Justice "Justice League: Cry for Justice")_ storyline, prior to the character's [relaunch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_52 "The New 52") alongside most of DC's properties in 2011.

Green Arrow was not initially a well-known character outside of comic book fandom: He had appeared in a single episode of the animated series _[Super Friends](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super\_Friends "Super Friends")_ in 1973. In the 2000s, the character appeared in a number of DC television properties, including the animated series _[Justice League Unlimited](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justice\_League\_Unlimited "Justice League Unlimited")_, _[Young Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Young\_Justice\_(TV\_series) "Young Justice (TV series)")_, _[The Batman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Batman\_(TV\_series) "The Batman (TV series)")_ and _[Batman: The Brave and the Bold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batman:\_The\_Brave\_and\_the\_Bold "Batman: The Brave and the Bold")_, and several [DC Universe Animated Original Movies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DC_Universe_Animated_Original_Movies "DC Universe Animated Original Movies"). In live action, he appeared in the series _[Smallville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smallville "Smallville")_, played by actor [Justin Hartley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justin_Hartley "Justin Hartley"), and became a core cast member. In 2012, the live action series _[Arrow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrow\_(TV\_series) "Arrow (TV series)")_ debuted on [The CW](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_CW "The CW"), in which the [title character](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Queen_(Arrowverse) "Oliver Queen (Arrowverse)") was portrayed by [Stephen Amell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Amell "Stephen Amell"), and launching several spin-off series, becoming the starting point for a shared television franchise called the [Arrowverse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrowverse "Arrowverse").

## Publication history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Green_Arrow&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Publication history")]

### Beginnings, 1941–1968

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Green_Arrow&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Beginnings, 1941–1968")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/c/cc/Green_Arrow_%26_Speedy_%28More_Fun_Comics_-73%29.png/250px-Green_Arrow_%26_Speedy_%28More_Fun_Comics_-73%29.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Green_Arrow_&_Speedy_(More_Fun_Comics_-73).png)

A panel of _More Fun Comics_ No. 73 (November 1941), featuring Green Arrow and Speedy's debut and their original costumes. Art by [George Papp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Papp "George Papp").

Green Arrow and [Speedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speedy_(comics) "Speedy (comics)") first appeared in _[More Fun Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/More\_Fun\_Comics "More Fun Comics")_ No. 73 ([cover-dated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Periodical_cover_date "Periodical cover date") November 1941), which was illustrated by artist [George Papp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Papp "George Papp"). When [Mort Weisinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mort_Weisinger "Mort Weisinger") was creating the character, aside from the obvious allusions to [Robin Hood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Hood "Robin Hood"), he took inspiration from a movie serial, _[The Green Archer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Green\_Archer\_(1940\_serial) "The Green Archer (1940 serial)")_, based on the novel by [Edgar Wallace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgar_Wallace "Edgar Wallace"). He retooled the concept into a superhero archer with obvious Batman influences.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-4) These include Green Arrow's [sidekick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidekick "Sidekick") Speedy, his use of an [Arrowcar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrowcar "Arrowcar") and Arrow-Plane for transportation, his use of an Arrow-Cave as his headquarters, his alter ego as a wealthy playboy, the use of an Arrow-Signal to summon him, as well as a clown-like arch foe named Bull's Eye, similar to Batman's arch-foe, [the Joker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joker_(character) "Joker (character)"). His and Speedy's first origin stories were told in _[More Fun Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/More\_Fun\_Comics "More Fun Comics")_ No. 89.

[![Image 6](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/b/bf/Green_Arrow_%28circa_the_1940s%29.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Green_Arrow_(circa_the_1940s).png)

Green Arrow, as he originally appeared during the 1940s, on the cover of _More Fun Comics_ No. 77 (March 1942). Art by Papp.

Green Arrow began as a back-up feature in _More Fun Comics_, but within four months the Green Arrow and Speedy replaced [Doctor Fate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_Fate "Doctor Fate") and [the Spectre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectre_(DC_Comics_character) "Spectre (DC Comics character)") as the cover feature. In _Superhero Comics of the Golden Age_, Mike Benton writes that "their front cover star status was probably due to Speedy's appeal – teenage sidekicks were the current rage."[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-benton-5) They were also given a spot as one of five back-up features to be promoted in one of the earliest team-up books, _[Leading Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leading\_Comics "Leading Comics")_, starting with issue No. 1 (Winter 1941). They appeared in _More Fun_ until issue No. 107 (January 1946), and then moved to _[Adventure Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adventure\_Comics "Adventure Comics")_ from No. 103 (April 1946) to No. 269 (February 1960).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-benton-5) Green Arrow and Speedy also appeared in various issues of _[World's Finest Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World's\_Finest\_Comics "World's Finest Comics")_ until issue No. 140 (March 1964).

He was one of the few DC characters to keep going after the [Golden Age of Comic Books](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Age_of_Comic_Books "Golden Age of Comic Books"). His longevity was due to the influence of creator Mort Weisinger, who kept him as a backup feature to the headlining [Superboy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superboy_(Kal-El) "Superboy (Kal-El)"), first in _More Fun Comics_ and then _Adventure Comics_; since [Superman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superman "Superman")-related titles were all but guaranteed success during this period. Green Arrow endured the 1940s and 1950s relatively unchanged, unlike most of his Golden Age contemporaries. As a result, he avoided being revived and "re-imagined" for the Silver Age, as [the Flash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flash_(DC_Comics_character) "Flash (DC Comics character)"), [Green Lantern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Lantern "Green Lantern"), and others were.

Aside from sharing _Adventure Comics_ with him, issue No. 258 featured an encounter between a younger Oliver Queen and Superboy. The Green Arrow and Speedy feature during this period included a short run in 1958 written by Dick and Dave Wood and drawn by [Jack Kirby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Kirby "Jack Kirby"). For much of this period, Green Arrow's adventures were written by [France Herron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France_Herron "France Herron"), who was the character's primary scripter 1947–1963.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-Herron-6)

### Neal Adams and Dennis O'Neil, 1969–1983

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Green_Arrow&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Neal Adams and Dennis O'Neil, 1969–1983")]

In 1969, artist [Neal Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neal_Adams "Neal Adams") updated the character's visual appearance by giving him a [Van Dyke beard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Dyke_beard "Van Dyke beard") and costume of his own design in _The Brave and the Bold_ No. 85 (August–September 1969).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-7) Writer [Dennis O'Neil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dennis_O'Neil "Dennis O'Neil") followed up on Green Arrow's new appearance by completely remaking the character's attitude in _Justice League of America_ #75 ([cover-dated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Periodical_cover_date "Periodical cover date") November 1969), having Oliver Queen lose his fortune and become an outspoken advocate of the underprivileged and the [political left wing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Left-wing_politics "Left-wing politics"). The story also turned teammate [Black Canary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Canary "Black Canary") into a love interest for Queen.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-back45-8)

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/f/f3/Green_lantern_76.JPG/250px-Green_lantern_76.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Green_lantern_76.JPG)

_Green Lantern_ (vol. 2) No. 76 (April 1970). Cover art by [Neal Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neal_Adams "Neal Adams").

In the early 1970s, Green Arrow became a co-feature with [Green Lantern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Lantern "Green Lantern") ([Hal Jordan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hal_Jordan "Hal Jordan")) in an acclaimed series of stories by O'Neil and Adams that dealt with various social and political issues. The two co-stars served to represent contrasting socio-political viewpoints: Green Arrow spoke for radical change while Green Lantern was an establishment liberal figure, wanting to work within existing institutions of government and law.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-back45-8) Queen convinces Jordan to see beyond his strict obedience to the [Green Lantern Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Lantern_Corps "Green Lantern Corps"), to help those who were neglected or discriminated against. O'Neil explained: "He would be a hot-tempered anarchist to contrast with the cerebral, sedate model citizen who was Green Lantern."[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-9) The duo embark on a quest in a beat-up [pickup truck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pickup_truck "Pickup truck") to "find America", along the way witnessing the problems of corruption, racism, pollution, as well as overpopulation confronting the nation. One story (in issues #78-79) was even widely interpreted as an allegory for the [Manson Family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manson_Family "Manson Family") cult murders, though O'Neil has emphasized that the story was about the [authoritarian left](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Authoritarian_left "Authoritarian left") and not Manson.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-back45-8)

In [_Green Lantern_ (vol. 2) #85–86](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snowbirds_Don't_Fly "Snowbirds Don't Fly"), it was revealed that Green Arrow's ward, [Speedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Harper_(character) "Roy Harper (character)"), was addicted to heroin.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-dc-ency-1) Speedy overcame his addiction with the help of the Black Canary. This story prompted a massive public reaction, including a congratulatory letter from the mayor of New York, [John Lindsay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lindsay "John Lindsay").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-back45-8) However, _Green Lantern_ sales had been in a major decline at the time Green Arrow was brought on as co-star, and the O'Neil/Adams stories failed to revive them.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-back45-8)_Green Lantern_ was canceled with issue No. 89 (April/May 1972), and the climactic story arc of the Green Lantern/Green Arrow series was published as a back-up feature in _[The Flash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flash\_(DC\_Comics\_character) "Flash (DC Comics character)")_ No. 217 through No. 219. In sharp contrast to the socially-relevant tales which preceded it, this story centered on emotional themes, with Green Arrow struggling to deal with the guilt of having killed a man.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-back45-8) Afterwards Green Arrow appeared in solo stories run as backups in _[Action Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Action\_Comics "Action Comics")_, starting with No. 421. [Elliot S. Maggin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliot_S._Maggin "Elliot S. Maggin"), who had made his comics debut with a Green Arrow story published in _Green Lantern_ (vol. 2) No. 87, was Green Arrow's writer for the next several years.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-back45-8)

In 1976, the _Green Lantern/Green Arrow_ title was re-launched, without the socially conscious themes of the original series, with O'Neil writing and [Mike Grell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Grell "Mike Grell") drawing. After the title moved to solo Green Lantern stories, solo Green Arrow stories appeared in _[World's Finest Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World's\_Finest\_Comics "World's Finest Comics")_. In his solo series, Oliver landed a job as a newspaper columnist, which allowed him to articulate his political beliefs in a more public field. In _World's Finest_ No. 255 (1979), Queen unsuccessfully ran for Mayor of Star City.

In May through August 1983, Green Arrow appeared for the first time in his own comic book, a four issue [limited series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limited_series_(comics) "Limited series (comics)").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-10) This miniseries introduced a running rivalry between Green Arrow and the supervillain [Count Vertigo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_Vertigo "Count Vertigo").

In 1985, the [Earth-Two](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth-Two "Earth-Two") Green Arrow died in the _[Crisis on Infinite Earths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crisis\_on\_Infinite\_Earths "Crisis on Infinite Earths")_, still wearing red boots and gloves. The [Golden Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Age "Golden Age") Earth-2 character had been retconned as a time-lost member of the original [Seven Soldiers of Victory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_Soldiers_of_Victory "Seven Soldiers of Victory") superhero team, recovered by the Justice League and Justice Society. After the Crisis, the Earth-Two Green Arrow and Speedy were retconned out of existence altogether, given the end of DC's former multiverse.

### Mike Grell's reinterpretation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Green_Arrow&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Mike Grell's reinterpretation")]

See also: [Green Arrow: The Longbow Hunters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow:_The_Longbow_Hunters "Green Arrow: The Longbow Hunters")

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/e/e9/Green_Arrow_The_Longbow_Hunters.jpg/250px-Green_Arrow_The_Longbow_Hunters.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Green_Arrow_The_Longbow_Hunters.jpg)

_Green Arrow: The Longbow Hunters_ #1, the gritty redefinition of Green Arrow. Cover by Mike Grell.

In 1987, DC Comics launched the character into a new ongoing title as part of their mature audience comic line. Written and illustrated by [Mike Grell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Grell "Mike Grell"), the revamp was launched with _[Green Arrow: The Longbow Hunters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green\_Arrow:\_The\_Longbow\_Hunters "Green Arrow: The Longbow Hunters")_ miniseries.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-11) In this three-issue [prestige format](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prestige_format "Prestige format")[limited series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limited_series_(comics) "Limited series (comics)"), a routine adventure against a group of drug runners led to tragedy as the Black Canary was captured and brutally tortured. In response, Oliver murdered his girlfriend's attackers. The miniseries also introduced the enigmatic female Japanese archer, [Shado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shado_(comics) "Shado (comics)"), whose family had suffered in a [World War II internment camp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese-American_internment "Japanese-American internment"). Shado later raped Oliver[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-12) and became pregnant by him, producing a son named Robert after [his father](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Queen "Robert Queen").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-13)

Under Grell, Green Arrow abandoned the use of his trademark gadget arrows and relocated from Star City to [Seattle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle "Seattle"), Washington. As the series was part of DC Comics' mature audience line, it took on a more gritty, violent, as well as urban tone, with Green Arrow often using deadly force against his enemies. Grell wrote the series for the first 80 issues, downplaying the super-hero aspects of the characters: Oliver abandoned his mask and was never actually referred to as "Green Arrow" and Black Canary was never shown using her sonic scream power (sometimes, this was explained as having lost it due to the events of _The Longbow Hunters_, though this was not consistent with her appearances in other titles published during this period). While crossover specials were conceived to allow other writers (most notably [Denny O'Neil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denny_O'Neil "Denny O'Neil"), who wrote _Batman_ and the mature audience comic _[The Question](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Question\_(character) "Question (character)")_) to use Green Arrow, Grell wrote him as largely isolated from the rest of the DC Universe; when other DC characters like longtime friend [Hal Jordan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hal_Jordan "Hal Jordan") (also known as [Green Lantern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Lantern "Green Lantern")) appeared, they did so in street clothes and used only their civilian names.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-14)

In place of the superhero community, Grell created his own supporting cast. In addition to Shado, Grell introduced Seattle police Lieutenant Jim Cameron, who was disgusted with Green Arrow's vigilante actions (including killing criminals), renegade [CIA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CIA "CIA") agent Greg Osborne, who began to monitor Queen's activities, as well as mercenary [Eddie Fyers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_Fyers "Eddie Fyers"), initially introduced as Queen's adversary, but later to become a companion of necessity when Green Arrow was forced to leave Seattle after false accusations of aiding terrorists. Grell's run ended with _Green Arrow_ vol. 2 No. 80, shortly after Dinah dumped Oliver.

During this period, the writer also redefined the character's origin in the four-part 1992 [limited series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limited_series_(comics) "Limited series (comics)"), _Green Arrow: The Wonder Year_. Grell portrayed Oliver Queen as a thrill-seeker who inherits his family business at a very young age. Changed by his sojourn on the island, Oliver decided to take up crime fighting as a means of rebelling against his responsibilities. During his first adventure in Star City, Oliver meets an old flame, Brianna Stone, a former college radical who warns him if he continued to carry his bow, he would one day have to use it for real. Grell's limited series also established Queen's attraction toward dangerous women.

### Post-Grell and character's temporary death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Green_Arrow&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Post-Grell and character's temporary death")]

[![Image 9](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/a/ab/Green_Arrows_%28Oliver_Queen_and_Connor_Hawke%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Green_Arrows_(Oliver_Queen_and_Connor_Hawke).jpg)

[Connor Hawke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connor_Hawke "Connor Hawke") and Oliver Queen as Green Arrows on the cover to _Green Arrow Secret Files & Origins_ No. 1 (December 2002). Art by [Matt Wagner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Wagner "Matt Wagner").

Once Grell left the series, DC almost immediately began restoring Green Arrow to the mainstream DC Universe. His ongoing series (mostly written by [Kelley Puckett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelley_Puckett "Kelley Puckett") and drawn by artist [Jim Aparo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Aparo "Jim Aparo")) was removed from the "Mature Audience" line (which had evolved into "[Vertigo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertigo_(DC_Comics) "Vertigo (DC Comics)")") with No. 63, prior to Grell's departure and Green Arrow began appearing in various super-hero titles as a guest: most notably _Green Lantern_ (vol. 3) #47, which had Oliver aiding Green Lantern in rescuing his longtime girlfriend [Carol Ferris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ferris "Carol Ferris") and her family from one of Hal's enemies, as well as the 1994 DC Comics miniseries _[Zero Hour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zero\_Hour:\_Crisis\_in\_Time "Zero Hour: Crisis in Time")_. In _Zero Hour_, where Hal Jordan seeks to remake the universe after the trauma of [Coast City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coast_City "Coast City")'s destruction drives him to destroy the Green Lantern Corps to gain the power to remake the universe, Queen is forced to shoot his old friend at a pivotal moment. Now tightly integrated in the DC Universe, the character [Connor Hawke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connor_Hawke "Connor Hawke") was introduced and revealed as Oliver Queen's son from a previous relationship.

In _Green Arrow_ (vol. 2) #100–101, Queen infiltrated a group of eco-terrorists known as the [Eden Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eden_Corps "Eden Corps") and sacrificed his life to prevent the group from detonating a bomb that would destroy the city of [Metropolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolis_(comics) "Metropolis (comics)").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-dc-ency-1) Superman attempted to intervene, but ultimately did not after Queen rebuked him for suggesting that Queen allow him to sever the arm attached to the bomb.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-15) The exchange between Queen and Superman pays tribute to Frank Miller's 1986 work _[The Dark Knight Returns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Dark\_Knight\_Returns "The Dark Knight Returns")_. Queen later admits in the _Quiver_ storyline (where he is resurrected) that he refused due to both his own issues at this point in his life and the more practical issue that he would be useless as an archer with one arm. Queen's death allowed the writers to shake up the status quo by making [Connor Hawke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow_(Connor_Hawke) "Green Arrow (Connor Hawke)") a replacement Green Arrow. The series, now written by [Chuck Dixon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuck_Dixon "Chuck Dixon"), would continue with Hawke as the main focus until issue No. 137, when the series was canceled.

### Smith, Hester and Parks/Meltzer 2000–2004

Queen is revived in 2000's, _Green Arrow_ (vol. 3) as part of the "[Quiver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quiver_(comics) "Quiver (comics)")" story arc, written by [Kevin Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Smith "Kevin Smith") and illustrated by [Phil Hester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Hester_(comics) "Phil Hester (comics)") and [Ande Parks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ande_Parks "Ande Parks"). It is revealed that Hal's resurrection of Oliver (seen on the last page of _Green Arrow_ (vol. 2) No. 137, the final issue of the Oliver/Connor ongoing series) was in reality a deliberately flawed one. In Hal's final hours before sacrificing his life to save the Earth during "[The Final Night](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Final_Night "The Final Night")", Hal speaks with Oliver's soul in the afterlife. The two agree to bring back _a_ version of Oliver Queen: one without a soul (so Oliver may properly stay in Heaven) and with no memory of the events of _The Longbow Hunters_ miniseries or of the subsequent events that followed, up until his death, Oliver reasoning that things went wrong for him after the events that drove him to kill for the first time and feeling that the copy of him was restored at the best point in his life.

For some years, this resurrected Oliver lives in Star City as a vigilante hero, completely under the radar of his other superhero friends, but eventually he is discovered and learns the truth of his resurrection, leaving the resurrected Oliver feeling uncertain about his state now that he knows he has no soul. His resurrection is eventually used by the grandfather of [Stanley Dover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Dover_(Arrow) "Stanley Dover (Arrow)") in an attempt to gain power over the monster that Dover accidentally bound to his grandson, Dover intending to take Oliver's body- possible only due to his lack of a soul- and use his access to the JLA's resources to find the monster. At the climax of the story, Oliver's soul returns from heaven, re-inhabits his resurrected earthly form and helps his son Connor Hawke fight a horde of demons, the body of Oliver having made contact with his soul and convincing him to return to save their son. Dover is defeated and actually consumed by the Beast, who then leaves of his own accord. Oliver also finds himself independently wealthy again, as Dover had transferred all his financial assets to Oliver in anticipation of taking over his body. He also picked up a new sidekick, [Mia Dearden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speedy_(Mia_Dearden) "Speedy (Mia Dearden)"), who would become the new Speedy, under Oliver's tutelage.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-16)

After the resurrection storyline, Smith wrote a second and shorter arc involving a super-powered serial killer, calling himself [Onomatopoeia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Onomatopoeia_(character) "Onomatopoeia (character)"), who sought to claim Connor as his latest victim. Smith then left the title and [Brad Meltzer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brad_Meltzer "Brad Meltzer") took over as writer.

Meltzer's single storyline for _Green Arrow_ featured Oliver and his former sidekick, [Roy Harper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Harper_(character) "Roy Harper (character)"), reuniting and going on a cross-country road trip to pick up old possessions of Oliver's, most notably a spare [Green Lantern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Lantern "Green Lantern") power ring entrusted to him by Hal Jordan many years earlier. The story also revealed that Oliver knew all along that Connor was his son and was even present at his birth, but that Oliver ultimately abandoned Connor and his mother, because of his fear of the responsibilities of fatherhood. Meltzer's storyline would continue into the miniseries _[Green Lantern: Rebirth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green\_Lantern:\_Rebirth "Green Lantern: Rebirth")_, which featured Oliver's attempts to use the ring against [Sinestro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinestro "Sinestro")- presumed dead for several years- before the ring is reclaimed by the reborn Hal Jordan.

Meltzer went on to write the miniseries _[Identity Crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Identity\_Crisis\_(DC\_Comics) "Identity Crisis (DC Comics)")_, which heavily featured Green Arrow as one of the story's main characters, investigating the murder of [Sue Dibny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_Dibny "Sue Dibny") – the wife of the [Elongated Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elongated_Man "Elongated Man") – and revealing that the League had been involved in mind-wiping various villains in the past to conceal their secret identities.

During this time, the character also appeared in a number of other titles, such as the _Justice League_, when he is temporarily brought into a 'reserve League' created by Batman after the original League is nearly killed by the powerful [Gamemnae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamemnae "Gamemnae"), and _[Justice League Elite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justice\_League\_Elite "Justice League Elite")_, where Oliver joins a 'black ops' super-team as the team's tactical consultant. His time in the Elite is notable for showing a brief affair with [Dawn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manitou_Dawn "Manitou Dawn"), the wife of the team's magical expert, [Manitou Raven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manitou_Raven "Manitou Raven").

### Judd Winick, 2004–2008

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Green_Arrow&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Judd Winick, 2004–2008")]

[Judd Winick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judd_Winick "Judd Winick") took over as _Green Arrow_'s writer and made many changes. [Mia Dearden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mia_Dearden "Mia Dearden"), the new Speedy, was revealed to be HIV positive, and attempts were made to expand Green Arrow's Rogues Gallery with [Merlyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merlyn_(DC_Comics) "Merlyn (DC Comics)") the archer, [Constantine Drakon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantine_Drakon "Constantine Drakon"), as well as Danny Brickwell (the [Brick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brick_(character) "Brick (character)")) joining the cast of existing Green Arrow villains such as the illusion-casting [Count Vertigo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_Vertigo "Count Vertigo") and the enigmatic [Onomatopoeia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Onomatopoeia_(character) "Onomatopoeia (character)"), the latter of whom, himself, was a relatively recent addition. Other DC villains, such as the [Riddler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riddler "Riddler"), made guest appearances throughout his run.

2006 saw the title (along with other DC comics titles) jump "[One Year Later](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Year_Later_(comics) "One Year Later (comics)")" after the events in _[Infinite Crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infinite\_Crisis "Infinite Crisis")_. Oliver, having once again amassed a large personal fortune, is the newly elected mayor of Star City, continuing his fight for justice both on the streets and within the political system.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-17) He also has a new costume, which appears to be a combination of the classic Neal Adams costume and the Mike Grell _Longbow Hunters_ costume. In flashbacks, it is revealed that Oliver survived a near-fatal attack during the events of the Infinite Crisis, as well as used his recuperation time to retrain. He works with several expert instructors including a sensei known as [Natas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natas_(character) "Natas (character)"), who also trained [Deathstroke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deathstroke "Deathstroke"), and becomes proficient in several martial arts including the use of swords, which he makes use of on occasion during this time, and proves that he and his family are now formidable combatants when battling Deathstroke and later Batman's rogue protégé [Jason Todd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Todd "Jason Todd"). He is eventually forced to resign from his position as mayor after a scandal where he learns that he had been secretly funding the [Outsiders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outsiders_(comics) "Outsiders (comics)"), essentially a bounty hunter team at this point in their history, coupled with his uncertain position with the voting public, having never had much more than 50% of the city on his side at a time. Queen is convinced to resign his position in exchange for his successor leaving the various social aid organisations and resources he had established alone, although Ollie was able to beat his opponent by resigning prior to the election and putting someone he trusted in charge of the city.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-18) The series concluded with Oliver proposing to Dinah ([Black Canary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Canary "Black Canary")).

In 2007, [Andy Diggle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Diggle "Andy Diggle") and [Jock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jock_(artist) "Jock (artist)")'s _[Green Arrow: Year One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green\_Arrow:\_Year\_One "Green Arrow: Year One")_[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-19) presented the newest official version of his origin. Using concepts from previous iterations, Oliver Queen is a rich, thrill-seeking activist who is attacked, thrown overboard and washes up on an island where he learns of a smuggling operation. Upon witnessing the inhabitants' slave-like living conditions, he begins to take down the smugglers' operation. He eventually returns to civilization changed by his experiences. In the final part of the story, Oliver claims that a mutiny or the actions of a group of heroin dealers could be used as a cover story for what transpired, referencing the original Green Arrow origin story, as well as Mike Grell's version.

### Green Arrow/Black Canary

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Green_Arrow&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Green Arrow/Black Canary")]

Main article: [Green Arrow and Black Canary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow_and_Black_Canary "Green Arrow and Black Canary")

After the end of the ongoing series, DC Comics published a four-part bi-monthly Black Canary miniseries in which Green Arrow teamed up with Black Canary to help get [Sin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sin_(DC_Comics) "Sin (DC Comics)") into school and establish a new life. This series concluded with the Black Canary accepting his proposal. This resulted in DC Comics publishing three interconnected specials revolving around the Green Arrow/Black Canary wedding that tied into that month's "[Countdown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Countdown_to_Final_Crisis "Countdown to Final Crisis")" stories. These were _The Black Canary Wedding Planner_, _JLA Wedding Special_, as well as _The Green Arrow/Black Canary Wedding Special_. The wedding special worked as a lead-in for a new _Green Arrow/Black Canary_ series. At the conclusion of the wedding special, the Black Canary is forced to kill Green Arrow after he appears to go mad and attacks her.

The new ongoing series picked up on this, quickly revealing that Green Arrow was alive (the dead Green Arrow being an [impostor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everyman_(DC_Comics) "Everyman (DC Comics)")) and being held hostage by "[Athena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granny_Goodness "Granny Goodness")". The Black Canary, Connor and Mia launch a rescue mission to save Green Arrow. As the team is united and on their way to safety, Connor is struck by a bullet meant for Oliver and is left in a vegetative state. While Connor rests, Oliver and Dinah go out and are officially married, since they had never actually been married in the _Wedding Special_, but they come home to find Connor has been kidnapped.

This storyline led directly into the second arc that followed the rescue of Connor from a mysterious foe. Connor is eventually found, now having recovered thanks to manipulation by [Doctor Sivana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_Sivana "Doctor Sivana"). With issue No. 15, Andrew Kreisberg took over as the series writer.

### _Blackest Night_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Green_Arrow&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Blackest Night")]

Oliver is transformed into a [Black Lantern Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Lantern_Corps "Black Lantern Corps") member and attacks his former allies, notably his son, wife and sidekick. During the battle, Connor says he never really forgave his father,[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-20) while Oliver's internal monologue reveals his thoughts, which express concerns for his "family" and disgust at his actions. The team manage to disable Oliver by freezing him with [liquid nitrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquid_nitrogen "Liquid nitrogen").

### _Cry for Justice_ and _Rise and Fall_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Green_Arrow&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Cry for Justice and Rise and Fall")]

In the [_Cry for Justice_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justice_League:_Cry_for_Justice "Justice League: Cry for Justice") miniseries, JLA foe [Prometheus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prometheus_(DC_Comics) "Prometheus (DC Comics)") destroys Star City, as part of a grand scheme to "hurt" the Justice League community of heroes. During the episode, the identity of the Green Arrow was nearly revealed by an old friend, Moreno. After tricking the Justice League into releasing him, Green Arrow tracks Prometheus to his hidden lair and kills him with a single arrow right between the eyes.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-21)

This murder, committed in secret, is what Oliver considers justice for the bombings (which also cost the life of [Lian Harper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lian_Harper "Lian Harper"), Roy Harper's (Red Arrow) daughter, who was killed in the bombing of Star City) and this immediately leads into the _Rise and Fall_ storyline, in which Oliver obsessively hunts other super-villains allied with Prometheus during the recent events,[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-22) including Prometheus's former allies who were involved in the bombing. When his JLA comrades learn of this plot, they confront Green Arrow and he realizes he has crossed a line and turns himself in: Black Canary returns her wedding ring and declares their marriage over. The _Green Arrow/Black Canary_ series ends during this story arc, as well as in the pages of _Justice League: Rise and Fall Special_; Oliver is tried, but found not guilty as most of the jury sympathise with his motives. He is exiled from Star City's remains as a result, choosing to live in the mysterious forest which has grown at its centre.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-23)

### _Brightest Day_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Green_Arrow&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Brightest Day")]

Following the events of _Blackest Night_, [Deadman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deadman_(character) "Deadman (character)") was brought to the ruins of Star City by his [white ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brightest_Day "Brightest Day"). Powered by the entity of life on Earth, the ring created a vast green forest, that instantly grew in the presence of the white light, in much of what remained of Star City.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-24)

Unbeknownst to the populace of Star City, Green Arrow returns and lives within the new forest, trying his best to protect a city still reeling from the death and destruction of Prometheus's attacks. With the law breaking down and numerous public figures being murdered, a new owner of Queen Industries, the result of a hostile takeover, arrives to enforce peace and rebuild the city.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-25) This self-proclaimed 'Queen' has a connection to Green Arrow's father and claims to be upholding the Queen family legacy where Oliver failed.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-26)

### The New 52

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Green_Arrow&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: The New 52")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/7/7b/Green_Arrow_%28The_New_52_version%29.jpg/250px-Green_Arrow_%28The_New_52_version%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Green_Arrow_(The_New_52_version).jpg)

The New 52 Green Arrow on the cover of _Green Arrow_ (vol. 5) No. 17 (February 2013). Art by Andrea Sorrentino.

In 2011, DC chose to relaunch its titles with new No. 1 issues and a refreshed continuity and called this initiative [The New 52](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_52 "The New 52"). _Green Arrow_ was one of 52 titles included in this.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-27) In the post-_[Flashpoint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flashpoint\_(comics) "Flashpoint (comics)")_ continuity, Oliver Queen is Green Arrow and he balances his own breaking of laws with his efforts to bring outlaws to justice across the globe. In the new continuity, Queen runs Q-Core, a communications technology company that is part of Queen Industries, through which he funds and armors himself as Green Arrow. He makes scarce allusion to his former partnership with [Roy Harper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Harper_(character) "Roy Harper (character)"), but Roy's memories in _Red Hood and the Outlaws_ establish that the pair fell out badly, leading Oliver to expel him from Q-Core, as well as prompting Roy's own downward spiral.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-28) He is based once again in Seattle and supported in his vigilante activities by a small team of close friends who are tech geniuses. In addition, his romantic history with the Black Canary, his friendship with Green Lantern (Hal Jordan), and his being a father (to both Connor Hawke and Shado's son Robert Queen II) did not take place as the result of the reboot.

The New 52 series was originally written by [J. T. Krul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._T._Krul "J. T. Krul"), who was later replaced by [Keith Giffen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Giffen "Keith Giffen") and [Dan Jurgens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Jurgens "Dan Jurgens"), who were in turn replaced by [Ann Nocenti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ann_Nocenti "Ann Nocenti"). None of these writers' runs were well received by critics or fans. Beginning with issue 17, the series received a new creative team in writer [Jeff Lemire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Lemire "Jeff Lemire") and artist Andrea Sorrentino, who brought more positive reception to the book. Lemire's story introduces new mysteries concerning Oliver's original time on the island where he was shipwrecked, as well as a central mythology concerning the ancient Arrow Clan and several other weapon-themed analogues to the Arrow, known as the Outsiders. New antagonists include Komodo, who Oliver learns was his father's archer apprentice and apparent murderer. It has also seen the New 52 debut of several characters, such as [Count Vertigo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_Vertigo "Count Vertigo"), [Shado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shado_(comics) "Shado (comics)"), the [Clock King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clock_King "Clock King"), [Richard Dragon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Dragon "Richard Dragon"), as well as John Diggle, a character originally created for the TV series _[Arrow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrow\_(TV\_series) "Arrow (TV series)")_.

When Oliver meets Shado, he learns she had a daughter from Oliver's father (Robert Queen) named Emiko, whom Komodo has raised as his own daughter. When Oliver returns to the island as part of his investigation into the Outsiders, and in search of a relic known as 'the green arrow', he discovers that his father had survived to the present, and disguised as one of Oliver's torturers on the island, he manipulated Oliver's time there, culminating in Oliver's transformation into the warrior he is today and the hero known as Green Arrow. Disgusted at this revelation, and taking the arrow relic with him, Oliver leaves Shado and his father behind, stranded on the island, before returning to America to take down the Outsiders. Shado and Robert followed Oliver to Prague, and Emiko turned against Komodo after learning the truth of her parentage. Robert was killed by Komodo in an attempt to save his daughter, and Komodo was later killed himself by Emiko.

From 2013, DC also chose to include Green Arrow as a headlining character in its _Justice League of America_ (vol. 3) series, which runs alongside _Justice League_ (vol. 2) and _Justice League Dark_. In this book, Queen is part of a crack state-sponsored team assembled by [Amanda Waller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amanda_Waller "Amanda Waller") and [Steve Trevor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Trevor "Steve Trevor") of [A.R.G.U.S.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A.R.G.U.S. "A.R.G.U.S.") to bring in good PR for the US government and serve as a defense against the independent Justice League headed by Superman and Batman should they ever go rogue. Following the cancellation of _JLA_ at the conclusion of the _[Forever Evil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forever\_Evil "Forever Evil")_ storyline, Green Arrow appears in its replacement series, _[Justice League United](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justice\_League\_United "Justice League United")_, also written by Lemire.

Lemire and Sorrentino left _Green Arrow_ after issue #34, to be replaced by writers [Andrew Kreisberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Kreisberg "Andrew Kreisberg") and Ben Sokolowski, and artist Daniel Sampere. Kreisberg was the executive producer of _Arrow_, and Sokolowski served as a writer for the show. Kreisberg and Sokolowski's first issue featured The New 52 debuts of [Felicity Smoak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felicity_Smoak "Felicity Smoak") and Mia Dearden, with Smoak modeled after her counterpart from _[Arrow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrow\_(TV\_series) "Arrow (TV series)")_.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Arrow#cite_note-29) Kreisberg's run saw Green Arrow face off against Mia's father, influential magnate John King, and [Merlyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merlyn_(DC_Comics) "Merlyn (DC Comics)"). At a moment of desperation given King's infinite resources and litany of loyal subjects, Smoak and Diggle recruit Batman, Arsenal, Emiko, [Katana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katana_(DC_Comics) "Katana (DC Comics)"), [Onyx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Onyx_(comics) "Onyx (comics)"), [Cupid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cupid_(DC_Comics) "Cupid (DC Comics)") and even [Lex Luthor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lex_Luthor "Lex Luthor"), at that time a Justice League member.

Following DC's _[Convergence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convergence\_(comics) "Convergence (comics)")_ storyline in April–May 2015, the title again received a new creative team in writer Ben Percy and artist [Patrick Zircher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Zircher "Patrick Zircher"), whose run was more influenced by the horror genre. Elements from _Arrow_ were removed, and characters created by Lemire, such as Emiko and Henry Fyff, were restored to major roles. Percy's first arc depicts Green Arrow confronting a racist serial killer using drone-like security technology in Seattle to systematically target criminals and potential criminals based on computer profiling and police data.
